But whoever first adorned this little fable with his lie imposed upon holy men, since in the books of the philosophers who wrote more carefully on the nature of things there is no trace of so remarkable a miracle. Not to mention that resurrection is beyond the powers of nature; that the pelican does not have a hooked beak but a very broad one, whence its Latin name platea; and that it is called not רחם from mercy but קאת from vomiting, as has been shown at length. Yet racham is the pelican not only for Arias, but also for Castellio and the Genevans. [III, 54] V. For Junius and Tremellius, however, רחם racham is the bee-eater. They hold, namely, that the bee-eater is called racham from love, because, as Pliny reports in book 10, chapter 33, it feeds its parents when they are hidden away. And Aelian says that for this reason the bee-eater is considered ^{c)} δικαιότερον [dikaioteron] (read δικαιότατον [dikaiotaton]) καὶ εὐσεβέστατον ὀρνίθων ἁπάντων [kai eusebestaton ornithōn hapantōn], the most just and most dutiful of all birds. Isidore too: Bee-eaters, the same as gauli, which are said to hide away and feed their parents. This is taken from Aristotle. For in History book 9, chapter 13, after [col. 302] describing the ἀντιπελαργία [antipelargia] of storks, he adds about bee-eaters: Φασὶ δέ τινες καὶ τοὺς μέροπας ταυτὸ τοῦτο ποιεῖν, καὶ ἀντεκτρέφεσθαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἐκγόνων, οὐ μόνον γηράσκοντας, ἀλλὰ καὶ εὐθὺς, ὅταν οἷοί τ᾽ ὦσι· τὸν δὲ πατέρα, καὶ τὴν μητέρα μένειν ἔνδον [Phasi de tines kai tous meropas tauto touto poiein, kai antektrephesthai hypo tōn ekgonōn, ou monon gēraskontas, alla kai euthys, hotan hoioi t᾽ ōsi; ton de patera, kai tēn mētera menein endon]. There are some who assert that bee-eaters also do the same, and are fed in turn by their young, not only when they are old, but as soon as the young are equal to this task: the father and mother remain inside. Note in passing that the Scholiast on Aristophanes' Birds writes τοὺς ἀέροπας [tous aeropas] instead of τοὺς μέροπας [tous meropas], and Suidas, under the word ἀντιπελαργεῖν [antipelargein], τοὺς ἀερόποδας [tous aeropodas], although both profess to follow Aristotle. And in Hesychius too you may read: Ἀέροπες· ἔθνος, etc. καὶ ὄρνεά τινα [Aeropes; ethnos, etc. kai ornea tina]. Aëropes: a people, and certain birds. And when Boeus, in book 2 of the Ornithog., says of Eumelus: Ἀπόλλων δὲ ὄρνιθα ἐποίησε τὸν παῖδα ἠέροπον, ὃς ἔτι νῦν τίκτει μὲν ὑπὸ γῆς, ἀεὶ δὲ μελετᾷ πέτεσθαι [Apollōn de ornitha epoiēse ton paida ēeropon, hos eti nyn tiktei men hypo gēs, aei de meleta petesthai]; Apollo changed the boy into the bird aëropus, which even now gives birth under the earth and is always striving to fly: by the name aëropus he means the bee-eater, about which the Philosopher says in History book 6, chapter 1: Ὃν δὲ οἱ Βοιώτιοι καλοῦσι μέροπα, εἰς τὰς ὀπὰς ἐν τῇ γῇ καταδυόμενος, νεοττεύει μόνος [Hon de hoi Boiōtioi kalousi meropa, eis tas opas en tē gē katadyomenos, neotteuei monos]; The bird which the Boeotians call merops alone goes down into holes in the earth to nest there. And in book 9, chapter 3: Τίκτει ἐν τοῖς κρημνοῖς τοῖς μαλακοῖς εἰσδύεται δὲ εἴσω καὶ τέτταρας πήχεις [Tiktei en tois krēmnois tois malakois eisdyetai de eisō kai tettaras pēcheis]; It breeds in the softer cliffs, going in as far as four cubits. And Pliny, book 10, chapter 33: They make their nurseries in the earth, being prevented by the weight of their bodies from seeking a high place. Hence bee-eaters were also called ἀέροπες [aeropes], ἀερόποδες [aeropodes] and ἠέροποι [ēeropoi]. Yet μέροπες [meropes] is correct, as these birds are so called because they have μεμερισμένην τὴν ὄπα, ὅ ἐστι τὴν φωνήν [memerismenēn tēn opa, ho esti tēn phōnēn]. Hence Probus on book 4 of the Georgics: MEROPES are so called in Greek because their voice admits of manifold division, from μερισμῷ ὀπὸς [merismō opos], that is, division of the voice.
